text.author: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court
text.title: Town of Concord v. Neil E Rasmussen & others, SJC-13721
text.summary1: (human1) In the court case SJC 13721, Town of Concord versus Neil Rasmussen and others, Attorney Gwen King, on behalf of the appellants, addresses the question of how a way becomes public and also how a public way is discontinued and ceases to be public, while Justice Kafka and other judges ask clarifying questions.
text.summary2: (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929; postedited) Attorney King, representing appellants in a dispute over whether a road remains public, argues that the 1932 discontinuance by Middlesex County Commissioners under section 32A could legally end the public status of ways, distinguishing this from section 21 town discontinuances, and questioning whether the way could have remained public through lost layout or prescription.
text.summary3: (gpt4o; postedited) Attorney Gwen King argues before Justices of the Court that the key issues in Town of Concord versus Neil Rasmussen involve how a way becomes public, how it is discontinued, and the legal distinctions between the relevant statutory sections, with emphasis on the public's access rights and the authority of county commissioners.
text.summary4: (Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct; postedited) Attorney Gwen King argues whether the 1932 discontinuance of a public way by the Middlesex County Commissioners under the 1924 act rendered it private.
text.summary5: (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; postedited) Attorney Gwen King argues before the Court whether the 1932 discontinuance by the Middlesex County Commissioners under the 1924 act legally discontinues a public way, and whether a way can be deemed public due to a lost layout, challenging the current interpretation of public way discontinuance laws.
